title: Dalmatian Black Risotto
description: Cuttlefish risotto stained through with its own ink. Everything about it is timing: the seafood and the rice have to finish in the same minute, and the ink goes in last so the colour is even.
notes: Ask the fishmonger to clean the cuttlefish and to keep the ink sacs for you. Sold separately, ink comes in 4 g sachets and two is right for this quantity.

steps.text: Cut the cleaned cuttlefish into strips about the width of a pencil.
steps.tip: Anything thicker cooks on a different clock than the rice and stays rubbery in a finished pan.

steps.text: Bring the fish stock to a bare simmer in a second pan and keep it there for the whole cook.
steps.tip: Cold stock stalls the pan every time you ladle. The rice stops releasing starch and never comes back.

steps.text: Sweat the onion and garlic in the olive oil until translucent, then add the cuttlefish and cook until it gives up its liquid and that liquid disappears again.
Stir in the arborio rice and toast it until the grains look glassy at the edges and chalky in the middle.
Pour in the white wine and let it cook away completely before any stock goes near the pan.
Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring, waiting each time until the pan is almost dry before the next.
Whisk the squid ink into the final ladle of stock and stir that through the rice.
steps.tip: Ink dropped straight into the pan streaks and stays streaked. Diluted first, it colours the whole thing in one turn of the spoon.

steps.text: Off the heat, beat in the cold butter and the Parmesan hard enough to make the risotto loose, season with salt and black pepper, and finish with parsley.
steps.tip: It should spread slowly on a tilted plate. If it holds a mound, it is too tight — another splash of stock.
